messages.text: How do changes in Wi-Fi 7/8 technology affect the measurement capability required from Signaling / Non-signaling Tester?

Wi‑Fi 7/8 push tester requirements mainly in **bandwidth, RF-chain count, signaling realism, and multi-technology integration**.

### 1) Signaling tester: from “single-link RF” to realistic multi-link behavior

For Wi‑Fi 7, **Multi-Link Operation (MLO)** is a key change. R&S source material says that RF TX/RX measurements for WLAN devices must be done under **real-world signaling conditions**, and because MLO is central to Wi‑Fi 7, the test environment needs **multiple RF chains**. The cited CMX500 setup is described as a **multi-technology, multi-channel signaling tester** with integrated Wi‑Fi 7 functionality, supporting Wi‑Fi 7 tests such as **2x2 MIMO, 6 GHz with out-of-band discovery, coexistence, embedded IP, and end-to-end testing**.  
Source: *Rohde & Schwarz presents its Wi‑Fi 7 multi-channel single-box test solutions for R&D and production at MWC 2024*; *Bluetest and Rohde & Schwarz collaborate to offer OTA testing of next-generation WLAN devices*.

**Impact:** A signaling tester now needs to emulate realistic AP/network behavior across multiple links and bands, not just generate/analyze one RF link.

### 2) Bandwidth and modulation requirements increase

Wi‑Fi 8 is described as retaining demanding Wi‑Fi 7 PHY parameters: **frequencies up to 7.125 GHz, channel bandwidths up to 320 MHz, 4096QAM, and MLO**, while adding new PHY/MAC technologies that create new testing hurdles.  
Source: *Rohde & Schwarz and Broadcom showcase first Wi‑Fi 8 RF signaling tests, paving way for next-gen connectivity*.

For non-signaling / RF production-style capability, the CMP180 is cited verifying a **480 MHz bandwidth waveform in loopback mode**, positioned as future-proof beyond Wi‑Fi 7.  
Source: *Rohde & Schwarz presents its Wi‑Fi 7 multi-channel single-box test solutions for R&D and production at MWC 2024*.

**Impact:** Testers need wider instantaneous bandwidth, higher modulation quality/EVM performance, and enough RF performance margin for 320 MHz / 4096QAM and beyond.

### 3) Wi‑Fi 8 adds early validation needs for new PHY/MAC features

R&S states that CMX500 has newly added **Wi‑Fi 8 / IEEE 802.11bn testing capabilities**, used with Broadcom to validate a prototype Wi‑Fi 8 device and showcase **physical-layer features unique to Wi‑Fi 8**. The raw source does not enumerate every new Wi‑Fi 8 feature, but it explicitly says Wi‑Fi 8 adds PHY/MAC technologies that create new testing hurdles.  
Source: *Rohde & Schwarz and Broadcom showcase first Wi‑Fi 8 RF signaling tests, paving way for next-gen connectivity*.

**Impact:** R&D signaling testers must support pre-standard/prototype validation, flexible waveform/protocol updates, and new PHY/MAC behavior before mass production test flows are stable.

### 4) OTA and antenna testing become more important

The sources note that WLAN device development requires measurement of **antenna, RF transmitter, and receiver characteristics** under real-world signaling conditions, and R&S collaborations combine OTA chambers with CMX500 for Wi‑Fi 7 assessment.  
Sources: *Bluetest and Rohde & Schwarz collaborate…*; *EMITE and Rohde & Schwarz join forces to support OTA measurements on Wi‑Fi 7 and 5G RedCap*.

**Impact:** Tester capability is no longer only conducted RF. It must fit OTA workflows for MIMO/MLO, antenna performance, coexistence, and end-to-end throughput/performance validation.

### 5) Non-signaling tester: production lines need speed, bandwidth, and parallelism

The raw battle-card evidence says that when factory lines need non-signaling test capability, R&S positions **CMP180 / CMP200 / CMW100** for that role.  
Source: *2026_02_CMX500_Amarisoft_Sales_Battle_Card*.

**Impact:** Non-signaling testers must prioritize fast calibration/verification, wideband waveform generation/analysis, multi-DUT or multi-port efficiency, and enough RF accuracy for Wi‑Fi 7/8 modulation and bandwidth.

---

### Bottom line

| Technology change | Required tester capability |
|---|---|
| Wi‑Fi 7 MLO | Multiple synchronized RF chains; multi-channel signaling |
| 6 GHz / up to 7.125 GHz operation | RF coverage through 6 GHz band and Wi‑Fi 6E/7/8 ranges |
| 320 MHz channels | Wide instantaneous bandwidth and analysis bandwidth |
| 4096QAM | Better EVM, phase noise, linearity, and RF accuracy |
| 2x2 MIMO / coexistence / E2E IP | Integrated protocol, IP throughput, and multi-radio test |
| Wi‑Fi 8 new PHY/MAC features | Flexible, upgradeable signaling platform for prototype validation |
| Production scaling | Non-signaling wideband testers such as CMP180/200/CMW100 class capability |

In short: **Wi‑Fi 7 makes multi-link, multi-chain signaling essential; Wi‑Fi 8 keeps those RF demands and adds new PHY/MAC validation challenges. Non-signaling testers must keep up with bandwidth, modulation accuracy, and production throughput, while signaling testers need realistic multi-link protocol and OTA capability.**

answer.text:
Wi‑Fi 7 increases tester requirements because MLO is a key feature, and testing it under real-world signaling conditions requires a test environment with multiple RF chains; the R&S CMX500 is described as a multi-technology, multi-channel signaling tester with integrated Wi‑Fi 7 functionality for such tests.[3][5] Wi‑Fi 7 testing also needs support for measurements such as RF TX/RX and antenna characteristics in signaling mode, plus Wi‑Fi 7-specific scenarios including 2x2 MIMO, 6 GHz operation with out-of-band discovery, coexistence, embedded IP, and end-to-end testing.[3][5]

Wi‑Fi 8 further raises the challenge because it retains demanding Wi‑Fi 7 physical-layer parameters—frequencies up to 7.125 GHz, channel bandwidths up to 320 MHz, 4096QAM, and MLO—while adding new PHY and MAC technologies that create new testing hurdles.[7] R&S states that the CMX500 now has Wi‑Fi 8 testing capabilities and can validate prototype Wi‑Fi 8 devices, including physical-layer features unique to Wi‑Fi 8.[1] The CMX500 is described as supporting WLAN including Wi‑Fi 7 and Wi‑Fi 8 in a single multi-technology signaling tester setup.[8]

For non-signaling production or factory testing, the RAW passages state that if non-signaling test capability is needed for factory lines, only R&S CMP180/200/CMW100 are indicated.[2] The R&S CMP180 is also shown verifying a 480 MHz signal waveform in loopback mode, described as future-proof for R&D and production beyond Wi‑Fi 7 requirements.[4]

cited_passages.text: [Wi-Fi 8](https://www.rohde-schwarz.com/us/solutions/wireless-communications-testing/wireless-standards/wlan-wi-fi/wi-fi-8-testing/wi-fi-8-testing_258504.html "Wi-Fi 8") builds upon the foundation of Wi-Fi 7, retaining core physical layer parameters like supported frequencies up to 7.125 GHz, channel bandwidths up to 320 MHz and 4096QAM modulation, as well as Multi-Link-Operation (MLO). However, to achieve its UHR goals, IEEE 802.11bn introduces a suite of innovative PHY and MAC layer technologies that present new testing hurdles. At MWC 2026, visitors can experience how to address key testing challenges associated with Wi-Fi 8 with the enhanced testing capabilities of the CMX500 one-box signaling tester, one of the most versatile mobile device test platforms in the market, which supports many of the demanding features of Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 today.

cited_passages.text: The CMX500 is a modular, powerful one-box signaling tester enabling comprehensive multi-technology testing. It covers LTE and NR in SA/NSA modes, NR-NTN, NB-NTN, Direct-to-Cell (D2C/DTC) testing and WLAN including Wi‑Fi 7 and Wi‑Fi 8. Consequently, the CMX500 allows R&D engineers of wireless devices to comprehensively test their design’s operation in both cellular and non-cellular standards of the latest generation in a single instrument setup.
